Big Fish in Small (and Big) Ponds: A Study of Careers

Jed DeVaro ,
Oliver Gürtler ,
Marc Gürtler ,
Christian Deutscher
The Journal of Law, Economics, and Organization, Volume 40, Issue 1, March 2024, Pages 76–107, https://doi.org/10.1093/jleo/ewac006
Published:
09 June 2022
  • PDF
  • Split View
  • Cite
  • Permissions Icon Permissions
  • Share Icon Share

Abstract

Talented, ambitious workers (big fish) often join highly competitive organizations (big ponds), though they sometimes instead choose less competitive organizations (small ponds) offering brighter promotion prospects. Big fish exist in both types of organizations, though average worker ability is higher in big ponds. Top executives enjoy higher wages in big ponds. Choosing a big pond allows workers to signal high ability. Workers sometimes overestimate or underestimate their abilities, choosing the wrong pond. Big ponds tend to be larger in total employment. All of the preceding phenomena are shown to be consistent with equilibrium in a new theoretical model of careers. (JEL J24, M53)

1. Introduction

Workers are closely attuned to future advancement opportunities when planning careers and choosing employers. Ambitious workers who are confident in their considerable talents sometimes choose to become “big fish in small ponds,”1 where promotion prospects are good. More often, however, such stars choose to become big fish in big ponds, meaning elite, competitive organizations with tough promotion standards.2 Their chances of rising to the upper echelons of the job hierarchy are relatively low in big ponds, but the potential rewards of doing so are high, because compensation for top executives tends to be higher in big than in small ponds. Thus, talented workers (i.e., “big fish”) exist in both types of organizations, though they are generally thought to be more heavily concentrated in big ponds, so that choosing a big pond allows workers to signal their high abilities to other potential employers. Moreover, big ponds (in the sense of prestige and competitiveness) tend to also be big in the sense of size, that is, total employment.

Although these ideas, including the fish-and-ponds terminology, are part of common parlance in discussions of careers, they have been absent from the theoretical literature on promotion and wage dynamics. The present study contributes to that literature by developing a theoretical model that exhibits fish-and-ponds phenomena as equilibrium behavior even when firms are ex ante identical.

In the two-period model, identical firms compete for workers who vary in their privately and imperfectly observed abilities. Firms’ job hierarchies have two levels and workers are hired into the subordinate job in the first period and might get promoted to a (higher paid) management job in the second period if their first-period performance reveals sufficiently high ability to their current employer. A worker’s output in each job level is linear in ability, with output being more sensitive to ability in the management job than in the subordinate job. In each job, output is also augmented by firm-specific human capital, which is accumulated in the first period of employment and lost if the worker switches firms in the second period.

The potential to switch firms arises because competing firms observe second-period job assignments and update their beliefs about the workers’ abilities accordingly. On the basis of those observations, competing firms make wage offers in attempts to poach the workers, whose original employers (who have learned their workers’ abilities at the end of the first period) can then make counteroffers in an effort to retain the workers. The presence of firm-specific human capital means that in most cases these counteroffers are sufficient to achieve retention in equilibrium. Separations occur in equilibrium only when a worker’s employer mistakenly fails to make a counteroffer, which is unlikely but possible.

The preceding setup is fairly standard in the promotions literature. The key feature that distinguishes the model from others is workers’ private information about their abilities. In particular, at the start of their careers, prior to joining a firm, workers observe a (possibly imperfect) signal of their abilities. Although worker heterogeneity in ability is standard in the literature, workers’ private information about ability is new and gives rise to the possibility that in equilibrium workers may sort across firms on the basis of this information. Workers who have high expected ability are “big fish” and those with low expected ability are “small fish.”3

Three equilibria arise. In the first, a symmetric pooling equilibrium, all firms use loose promotion rules in which every worker is promoted in the second period. This equilibrium always exists and is unique if firm-specific human capital is sufficiently important. In the second, a symmetric separating equilibrium, all firms use stringent promotion rules in which only the high-ability workers are promoted in the second period. Existence of this equilibrium requires that firm-specific human capital not be too important.

The third and most interesting is an asymmetric equilibrium, which shall henceforth be called the “fish-and-ponds equilibrium.” In that equilibrium, some firms (i.e., big ponds) use stringent rules in which only high-ability workers are promoted, whereas other firms (i.e., small ponds) use loose rules in which everyone gets promoted and workers sort across firms accordingly based on their private information about their abilities. The fish-and-ponds equilibrium exists only when firm-specific human capital is neither too important (in which case all firms would want to promote all of their workers) nor too unimportant (in which case the small pond would not want to promote all of its workers). In the fish-and-ponds equilibrium, promoted workers receive higher wages in big ponds than in small ones, which happens because being promoted in a big pond is a positive signal of ability, both because the worker initially chose a pond with a more stringent promotion rule and because the worker managed to achieve a promotion in that challenging environment.

The second and third equilibria are characterized by inefficient job assignments, because some workers are not promoted even though they would be more productive in the management job. The logic follows Waldman (1984). When a worker’s ability is observed by the initial employer but not by competing ones, promotions signal high ability and induce competing firms to increase their wage offers to promoted workers. The initial employer must match the competing wage offers to retain promoted workers. To avoid this cost, the initial employer withholds promotions from “marginal” workers who would be only slightly more productive if promoted than if retained in their current job, thereby reaping the benefits of private information about these workers’ abilities.

The fish-and-ponds equilibrium has four empirical implications that are consistent with observation. First, big and small ponds can coexist in equilibrium, a result that has not been shown in the prior theoretical literature on promotions. Second, workers who receive favorable ability signals choose big ponds, whereas workers who receive unfavorable ability signals choose small ponds. Third, both high- and low-ability workers (in the sense of realized ability) can be found in both types of ponds. Fourth, managerial wage levels are higher in big than in small ponds.

The accounting industry offers an example that illustrates all of these implications. The “Big Four” accounting firms are big ponds and they coexist in the industry with numerous smaller accounting firms of lesser repute in which the promotion standards are more relaxed. Early-career workers who have received strong positive signals about their abilities (e.g., high grade point averages in business programs or high scores on the Certified Public Accountant Examination) tend to select disproportionately into the prestigious Big Four. Nonetheless, highly talented accountants can be found outside of the Big Four and not all accountants in the Big Four turn out to be stars. Finally, managerial pay is higher within the Big Four than in lesser accounting firms.

In addition to rationalizing the fish-and-ponds phenomenon in a model with ex ante identical firms, the theoretical model and its extensions exhibit a number of implications that are consistent with empirical evidence and that are discussed in Section 5. Thus, a contribution of the fish-and-ponds theoretical framework presented here is that it can explain and deepen our understanding of a pattern of empirical evidence, thereby distinguishing it from the theoretical studies discussed in the next section, whose approaches to the “ponds idea” are less focused on, and less easily connected to, empirical evidence.

2. Related Literature

In Spence (1973), workers have private information about their abilities, which they signal to prospective employers. In Waldman (1984), employers have private information about their workers’ abilities, which they signal to competing employers by promoting (or not promoting) their workers. The present study merges both types of private information into a single model.

The study contributes to the promotion signaling literature, which to date has not addressed the fish-and-ponds phenomenon.4 A key idea in that literature is inefficiency in job assignments, whereby some workers who would be more productive in the managerial job are inefficiently denied promotion by their employer so as to avoid the costly wage increase that would be required to retain such workers when competing firms infer from their promotions that these workers have high ability. This inefficiency has been shown to vary across worker groups based on educational attainment, race, gender, and age, which forms the basis for a recent empirical literature that supports promotion signaling (e.g., Okamura 2011; DeVaro and Waldman 2012; Bognanno and Melero 2015; Cassidy et al. 2016; Dato et al. 2016; DeVaro et al. 2018).

From the standpoint of the present analysis, a particularly relevant study in the promotion signaling literature is Waldman (2016). That study, like ours, incorporates promotion signaling and workers’ private information about their abilities. A key respect in which the two studies differ concerns the way in which workers signal their privately observed abilities. In Waldman’s model, they do it via their educational investment choices, whereas here they do it via their decisions to join big or small ponds.

Zábojník and Bernhardt (2001) generate an equilibrium in which firms vary in size and, therefore, in how promotion signaling outcomes vary with firm size. Their model differs from the present one in several respects. Firms differ by productivity level, and workers are ex ante identical, whereas in the present study firms are ex ante identical and workers privately observe a signal of their own ability. Moreover, in the present equilibrium, workers (based on their own traits) select into ponds, whereas in the Zábojník and Bernhardt (2001) equilibrium workers are indifferent between joining high-productivity and low-productivity firms, so there is no self-selection of heterogeneous workers into firms. Large firms do not set higher promotion standards than small firms in this equilibrium; in either type of firm, the worker with the highest accumulated human capital after one period gets promoted. In contrast, in the present model, promotion standards are endogenously determined in equilibrium and are higher in big than in small ponds, despite all firms being ex ante identical.

Building on the efficiency wage model of Shapiro and Stiglitz (1984) rather than on the promotion signaling framework, Ke et al. (2018) construct a model in which a firm’s characteristics, such as its technology, drive its choice of personnel policies. This in turn means that workers’ careers might evolve differently according to which firm they join, as is the case in the present study in which workers’ careers differ according to whether they join big or small ponds. In Ke et al. (2018), workers who join firms with larger spans of control are more likely to start their careers at the bottom rung of the job hierarchy, where they will enjoy better relative pay but at the expense of having more limited promotion prospects and less post-promotion job security.

Turning to work that more directly relates to the fish-and-ponds phenomenon, Frank (1984a, 1984b) considers settings in which workers sort across firms according to their abilities. In those studies, workers derive utility from both consumption and their relative place in the income hierarchy of their employer. As a result, high-ability workers join firms that also employ low-ability workers in order to obtain a higher status than that obtained with an employer that employs only workers of similar abilities. These workers choose to be big fish in small ponds. Frank also shows that high-ability workers are willing to accept a lower wage in order to enjoy a higher status, and by doing so subsidize low-ability workers who are paid above their marginal output.

Morgan et al. (2018) study self-selection into contests to explore the question of whether it is better to be a big fish in a small pond or a small fish in a big pond. Their analysis differs from the present one in a number of respects. There is no job hierarchy, prizes are exogenous parameters attached to ponds, and ponds do not compete with each other for contestants. In contrast, the present analysis contributes to the promotion and wage dynamics literature, with a job hierarchy explicitly modeled and promotion prizes that are the endogenous wage offers that result from competition among employers in a market-based setting. Other studies that address the fish-and-ponds phenomenon, but without explicitly modeling a job hierarchy to analyze promotions in organizations, include Azmat and Möller (2009, 2018), Leuven et al. (2010, 2011), and Konrad and Kovenock (2012).

In a pair of related papers, Damiano et al. (2010, 2012) study sorting across organizations when workers care about the average ability of their peers (i.e., a peer effect) and about their relative ranking among their peers. The present model differs by featuring a job hierarchy with mobility across hierarchical levels, the potential for cross-firm mobility, and wage offers (and counteroffers) that are not limited to allocation of an exogenous fixed budget.

The theoretical model shares some common elements with that of Deutscher et al. (2020). In particular, workers sort across firms on the basis of privately observed signals about their abilities, and both big and small ponds exist in equilibrium. The employer is passive in that model, with no role other than to promote the best performer of its two employees. In contrast, employers in the present model choose entry-level wages and promotion rules endogenously, which implies a more complex model and analysis. Big-pond firms deliberately opt for (inefficiently) strict promotion rules to attract only the workers who are confident that they have high ability. And in contrast to the signaling literature, workers sort across firms. The present model overcomes two further limitations of Deutscher et al. (2020). First, in that model the firm always hires exactly two workers, so big and small ponds are always the same size. Second, that model ignores all of the parameters that typically play a role in promotion signaling models, for example, those relating to the production functions and those concerning firm-specific human capital.

The related empirical study by Gong et al. (2018) compares the career outcomes of soccer players from teams that were relegated from the English Premier League to those that just escaped relegation, finding that young players actually benefited from their teams being relegated. In contrast to Gong et al. (2018), the present study focuses on the signaling effects of choosing to work for a specific type of firm. Workers who are confident of having high ability are found to benefit from joining big-pond firms, as they can signal their high ability by doing so.

3. A Model of Promotions with Workers’ Private Information about Ability

3.1 Model Setup

The labor market is competitive, with firms competing for workers’ services. There are two periods, t∈{1,2}⁠, with no discounting. There are N≥4 identical firms and a (countable) set W of workers. All parties are risk neutral. Each firm has a hierarchy with two jobs (a low-level job 1 and a high-level job 2), where jobs are indexed by k∈{1,2}⁠. Long-term contracts that bind workers to their initial firm for both periods are infeasible, as are explicit incentive schemes that link pay to performance. These are standard simplifying assumptions adopted in, for example, Zábojník and Bernhardt (2001), Gibbons and Waldman (1999, 2006), and DeVaro and Waldman (2012).

The absence of worker effort choices requires some comment, given that big ponds are characterized by long working hours, which represent one way in which effort is supplied. The problem of incentivizing workers to exert effort is arguably separable from the matching of workers into firms. Suppose that the model incorporated workers’ effort and that there was some objective measure of effort (but not of ability) that could be used in an explicit incentive contract. Then the problem of incentivizing workers to exert effort would be independent of the selection issues investigated here, so it could be disregarded without affecting the main results.5

At the start of period 1, Nature chooses each worker’s ability level. Let aj denote worker j’s ability, which has possible realizations aL and aH (with 0<aL<aH⁠). Ability aj is initially unknown to all firms and workers. Worker j, however, observes some (possibly imperfect) signal σj about their ability. The possible signal realizations are σL and σσσH(≠σL)⁠. It is assumed that σσλP(aH|σH)=P(aL|σL)=λ∈(1/2,1] and σσλP(aH|σL)=P(aL|σH)=1−λ⁠, though the model’s results would also hold with a more general information structure. The higher is λ, the better informed the worker is about their own ability. If λ = 1, the worker knows their ability perfectly. Let pH denote the probability that σσσj=σH and pL the probability that σσσj=σL⁠, where pH+pL=1⁠.

After abilities are assigned by Nature and workers observe their ability signals, firms make wage offers to attract workers into period-1 employment and these offers are observable by all firms. Workers must perform job 1 before being able to perform job 2, implying that workers are assigned to job 1 in period 1. Some may ultimately be promoted to job 2 at the end of period 1, according to promotion rules to be explained shortly. Each firm’s number of positions in both types of jobs is unconstrained, so that all workers who perform sufficiently well in job 1 can and will be promoted. Under this assumption, all of the workers are hired and promoted independently of each other, so that attention can be restricted to a representative worker, j. The output of worker j∈W who is employed by firm i∈{1,…,N} in period t and assigned to job k is

(1)

Following Waldman (1984), we assume d2>d1>0 (and 0≤c2<c1⁠), so that output is more responsive to ability in job 2 than in job 1. Furthermore, sijt∈{0,S} is an indicator variable capturing firm-specific human capital acquired in period 1. It equals zero in period 1 and also in period 2 if worker j has switched firms after period 1. It equals S > 0 in period 2 if the worker remains with the period-1 firm.

At the end of period 1, the worker’s employer observes the worker’s output and then assigns the worker to a job in period 2. Given that the employer observes all parameters of the production function, observing the worker’s output also allows the employer to observe the worker’s ability.6 Thus, promotion rules can be stated in terms of observed ability. The parameter aH is assumed to be sufficiently high that a firm always promotes a worker who is revealed to have high ability. Competing firms cannot observe individual outputs (or, therefore, abilities) but can observe the worker’s period-2 job assignment, using this information to update their ability assessment for the worker. The condition c2+d2aL≥c1+d1aL is maintained throughout the analysis and ensures that, from an efficiency perspective, a worker should always be promoted regardless of ability.

At the start of period 2, the external firms attempt to hire the worker by making wage offers, whereas the current employer tries to retain the worker. The external firms move first by simultaneously making wage offers. The incumbent employer observes these wage offers and can then make a counteroffer. Each worker is hired by the firm making the highest offer. Ties are broken randomly, except for the case in which the period-1 employer is among the firms making the highest offer, in which case the worker remains with the initial employer. It is assumed that S is sufficiently high so that, in equilibrium, the external firms never succeed in hiring workers away from the period-1 employer, with the following exception. As in DeVaro and Waldman (2012), there is a probability, γ, that the incumbent firm mistakenly fails to make a counteroffer and which is independent of the workers’ abilities. The assumption ensures that external firms poach workers with positive probability, implying that the highest equilibrium offer by an external firm equals the worker’s expected productivity.7 The solution concept is Perfect Bayesian equilibrium. 3.2 Characterization of the Symmetric Equilibria

Since all firms have the same production technology, it is unsurprising that a symmetric equilibrium can exist in which they all make the same period-1 wage offers and use the same promotion rule. Given the assumption that firms wish to promote workers who are revealed to have high ability, two such equilibria can exist. They are presented in the following Propositions 1 and 2.

Before turning to these propositions, we briefly explain how decisions are made in our model and which conditions must be fulfilled in equilibrium. In period 2, the incumbent firm always matches the highest offer by the external firms, meaning that it will always retain the worker unless it mistakenly fails to make a counteroffer. The external firms, anticipating this reaction, thus compete in regular Bertrand fashion and their highest offer equals the output that they expect the worker to produce. This output depends on the external firms’ expectation of the worker’s ability which, in turn, depends on whether or not the worker was promoted and the (promotion) strategy that the external firms believe the incumbent to play (and which they correctly infer in equilibrium).

The incumbent firm promotes the worker if and only if the profit (i.e., output minus wage) from promotion is higher than the profit from reassigning the worker to the low-level job. Both output and wage are typically larger in the high-level job than in the low-level job so that the firm needs to trade off the larger output and the larger wage when making the promotion decision.8 Finally, in period 1, firms again compete in Bertrand fashion, implying that all rents accrue to the workers. Workers’ selection of firms is not an issue in the symmetric equilibria and we elaborate on it when presenting the asymmetric equilibrium in the next subsection.

In the symmetric pooling equilibrium described in Proposition 1, all firms use loose promotion rules, promoting all workers regardless of their abilities.

 
Proposition 1

There is a nonempty set of parameters under which there exists a symmetric pooling equilibrium (henceforth the “loose equilibrium”) with the following properties:

  • In period 1, all firms offer each worker a wage of w1l⁠.

  • Each worker accepts each of the offers with the same probability, 1N⁠.

  • At the end of period 1, each worker is promoted to job 2. All firms offer the worker a period-2 wage of w2l⁠.

  • With probability γ1−γ⁠, the worker accepts their period-1 employer’s offer. With probability γ, the worker randomly accepts an external firm’s offer.

Proofs of all propositions are in Appendix A and contain the expressions for equilibrium wages and the parameter constellations for which the equilibria exist. In all propositions, references to “all firms” making a particular period-2 wage offer have the caveat that there is a (small) probability that the incumbent firm mistakenly fails to make a counteroffer.

The symmetric pooling equilibrium described in Proposition 1 always exists whenever S is sufficiently large, meaning when firm-specific human capital is sufficiently important. The reason is that external firms’ wage offers do not depend on S, because firm-specific human capital is lost when a worker switches firms. A worker’s current employer bases the wage offer on the external firms’ offers, so the current employer’s offer does not depend on S either. Moreover, the worker’s productivity advantage in job 2 compared with job 1 is increasing without bound in S. Therefore, whenever S is high enough, all firms always wish to promote all of their workers independent of their abilities. The equilibrium described in Proposition 1 maximizes welfare for the following reason. Having worked in job 1 in period 1, workers are always more productive in job 2 than in job 1. Hence, the overall surplus is maximized when all workers are assigned to job 2 in period 2. Proposition 1 could be interpreted as describing a seniority-based promotion system, as discussed in Section 5.

It is instructive to relate our results to those of Rothschild and Stiglitz (1976). They model a competitive insurance market, where customers are either good or bad risks (i.e., they have low or high probability of causing damage) and they are privately informed about their type. Rothschild and Stiglitz (1976) show that a pooling equilibrium in which both types of customers are offered the same insurance contract does not exist. The intuition is that firms can make a profit by deviating and offering an alternative contract that is only attractive to the good-risk customers.

Transferring their intuition to our model, one might conjecture that a pooling equilibrium does not exist either, since firms have an incentive to deviate by offering contracts that only appeal to the workers observing a positive signal about their ability. Such a contract would need to stipulate a relatively lower promotion probability in case a worker has low ability, since changing the promotion decision is the only possible way to separate worker types.

There are two important differences between our model and that of Rothschild and Stiglitz (1976). First, in their model firms can commit to insurance contracts, whereas they cannot commit to promotion rules in ours. This means that firms cannot deviate by claiming that they are not going to promote low-ability workers if it is actually optimal for firms to promote these workers. Second, the insurance contracts studied by Rothschild and Stiglitz (1976) are continuous in the sense that the payments that customers receive can be continuously varied. In our model, in contrast, the promotion decision is discrete. As a consequence of the preceding two differences, the aforementioned deviation is not possible in our model. Thus, a pooling equilibrium can exist.

If we were to adopt their assumptions by allowing firms to commit to continuous promotion rules (i.e., rules that allow workers to be promoted with certain pre-specified probabilities), then the pooling equilibrium described in the preceding proposition would fail to exist. The reason is that, under these assumptions, firms would indeed be able to offer alternative contracts that are only attractive to the workers observing positive signals about their abilities, meaning that a deviation to such an alternative contract is beneficial.

The next proposition shows that inefficient equilibria can also exist. In the forthcoming equilibrium, promotion rules are more stringent than in the preceding equilibrium, meaning that only high-ability workers are promoted. Therefore, a worker’s period-2 job assignment always reveals the worker’s ability to all firms. Consequently, promoted workers’ wages are higher than those of non-promoted workers, which, as in Waldman (1984), makes it optimal for the firms to set an inefficiently high promotion standard. Existence of a symmetric separating equilibrium in which only high-ability workers are promoted requires that S not be too large given that, as stated in the discussion following Proposition 1, if S is sufficiently large, firms wish to promote all workers, regardless of their abilities.

 
Proposition 2

There is a nonempty set of parameters under which there exists a symmetric separating equilibrium (henceforth the “stringent equilibrium”) with the following properties:

  • In period 1, all firms offer each worker a wage of w1s⁠.

  • Each worker accepts each of the offers with the same probability, 1N⁠.

  • At the end of period 1, a worker j is promoted if and only if aj = aH. All firms offer a wage of w22s if the worker is promoted and w21s if the worker is not promoted.

  • With probability γ1−γ⁠, the worker accepts their period-1 employer’s offer. With probability γ, the worker randomly accepts an external firm’s offer.

3.3 Characterization of the Asymmetric “Fish-and-Ponds” Equilibrium

Within each of the preceding two symmetric equilibria, all firms behave identically, so that workers’ self-selection into firms does not play a role. Self-selection becomes relevant only if firms differ in their decisions and workers then select a firm that offers the highest expected lifetime earnings (i.e., the sum of the period-1 wage and the expected period-2 wage). Interestingly, even though all firms have the same production technology, asymmetric equilibria potentially exist. In particular, it is possible that some firms (i.e., big ponds) select stringent promotion rules, promoting only workers who are revealed to have high ability, whereas other firms (i.e., small ponds) promote all workers regardless of their ability. The following proposition characterizes the corresponding asymmetric separating fish-and-ponds equilibrium.

 
Proposition 3

There is a nonempty set of parameters under which there exists an asymmetric separating equilibrium (henceforth the “fish-and-ponds equilibrium”) with the following properties:

(a) In period 1, small-pond firms i∈{1,…,ı^} (with ı^∈{2,…,N−2}⁠) all offer each worker a wage of w1SP⁠, whereas big-pond firms i∈{ı^+1,…,N} all offer a wage of w1BP⁠.

(b) If σσσj=σL⁠, worker j accepts each offer of small-pond firms i∈{1,…,ı^} with the same probability, 1ı^⁠. If σσσj=σH⁠, worker j accepts each offer of big-pond firms i∈{ı^+1,…,N} with the same probability, 1N−ı^⁠.

(c) (i) When worker j is hired by some small-pond firm i∈{1,…,ı^}⁠, this firm always promotes the worker at the end of period 1.

(ii) All firms offer the worker a period-2 wage of w2SP⁠.

(iii) When worker j is hired by some big-pond firm i∈{ı^+1,…,N}⁠, this firm promotes the worker at the end of period 1 if and only if aj = aH.

(iv) If the worker is promoted, all firms offer the worker a period-2 wage of w22BP(>w2SP)⁠. If the worker is not promoted, all firms offer a wage of w21BP(<w22BP)⁠.

(d) With probability γ1−γ⁠, the worker accepts their period-1 employer’s offer. With probability γ, the worker randomly accepts an external firm’s offer.

In the fish-and-ponds equilibrium, a firm is defined as a small pond if it chooses to promote workers regardless of their abilities, whereas a firm is a big pond if it promotes only those workers who are revealed to have high ability. Pond size is defined in terms of unconditional promotion probabilities, meaning that a small pond has a high unconditional probability of promotion and a big pond has a low unconditional probability of promotion. An alternative definition of pond size would condition on ability. That is, holding worker type/ability fixed, a small pond has a larger promotion probability, and a large pond has a smaller probability. This alternative (conditional) definition applies in the preceding fish-and-ponds equilibrium, albeit only weakly. In the equilibrium, the condition is true for low-ability workers, because those workers are never promoted in the big pond but are always promoted in the small pond. High-ability workers are always promoted in either pond, so their promotion probabilities are the same. Thus, conditional on ability, the overall promotion probability is weakly lower in the big than in the small pond. Moreover, when conditioning on the ability signals rather than on their realizations, the inequalities are strict for both signals.

There is no assumption that a firm’s promotion strategy is observable to other employers, though firms correctly infer other firms’ promotion rules in equilibrium from their period-1 wage offers. Workers self-select into firms, choosing a small pond when receiving an unfavorable ability signal (i.e., σσσj=σL⁠). The reason is that a worker fears that if they select a big pond they might not be promoted, in which case the worker’s low ability would be revealed to the market. In contrast, a worker receiving a favorable ability signal (i.e., σσσj=σH⁠) is sufficiently confident about prevailing in the big pond that selecting the big pond is optimal.

An implication is that ponds are signals. Choosing a big pond allows workers to signal high ability in two ways. First, only workers with a favorable ability signal select a big pond and this is reflected in period-1 wages, as discussed below. Second, only those workers who are revealed to have high ability will be promoted. Consequently, big ponds pay higher period-2 wages than small ponds (in job 2). The respective wages in job 1 cannot be compared across ponds, because in a small pond, all workers are promoted in equilibrium. As discussed at the start of Section 4, however, the model could be extended to allow for an additional ability level for which it would be inefficient to promote a worker. In that case, a small pond would be a firm in which workers are promoted unless they have the lowest ability, whereas a big pond would be a firm in which only the workers of the highest ability are promoted.

It is also possible that period-1 wages are higher in big than in small ponds, though there are two opposing effects. Firms compete for the workers’ services, so all rents accrue to the workers, implying that period-1 wages depend on the total output a worker is expected to produce in both periods. Promotion rules are efficient in small ponds, whereas higher-ability workers self-select into big ponds. Because of the former result, a worker’s total output tends to be relatively larger in a small pond than in a big one, and because of the latter it tends to be larger in the big pond. If the latter effect dominates, period-1 wages are higher in big than in small ponds. The sum of the period-1 wage and the period-2 wage in job 2 is always higher in the big than in the small pond. This follows from λλw1BP+w22BP≥w1BP+λw22BP+(1−λ)w21BP≥w1SP+w2SP⁠, where the first inequality is strict for λλ<1 (and the second follows from Condition (A8) in Appendix A).

In the fish-and-ponds equilibrium of Proposition 3, the selection of workers into firms is determined by worker choices. In certain real-world settings, however, employer screening and selection are likely to be important. For example, many MBAs want to work for the two big-pond consulting firms, McKinsey and Bain, which allows those firms to be highly selective. Employer screening and selection is a relevant consideration that should be explored in future work. Nonetheless, analysis of the ponds phenomenon from the standpoint of worker choice is still enlightening, even in the preceding example. While the yield rate on job offers extended by big-pond consulting firms is surely high, it is not 100%; some workers turn those offers down if they prefer a less competitive working environment where their chances of standing out and advancing quickly within the firm are higher. Moreover, the observed yield rate is inflated because there are some talented MBAs who could successfully compete for jobs at Bain or McKinsey but who select out by not even applying. We view worker self-selection into firms as an important aspect of the ponds phenomenon even if it cannot account for it entirely.

Turning next to equilibrium existence, the first question is whether pure-strategy equilibria exist that exhibit promotion rules that differ from the three identified in the preceding propositions. The answer is no, as long as it is assumed that firms treat workers with identical output realizations the same way by holding them to the same promotion rule.9 One qualification should be noted, however. Given that firms make zero profits in equilibrium, alternative pure-strategy equilibria may exist in which some firms make lower wage offers and never hire any workers, while the remaining firms make the same offers as in the present model. But in that case the outcomes concerning equilibrium job assignments and wages would be unchanged even if some firms play different strategies, so from an empirical standpoint such equilibria would look identical to those presented.10

The following corollary to Propositions 1–3 relates the existence of the fish-and-ponds equilibrium to that of the stringent and loose equilibria.

 

Corollary 1. The existence of the fish-and-ponds equilibrium implies the existence of the stringent equilibrium, whereas it does not imply the existence of the loose equilibrium.

Whenever the fish-and-ponds equilibrium exists, the stringent equilibrium also exists.11 The intuition is that, upon learning workers’ abilities at the end of period 1, the big-pond firms in the fish-and-ponds equilibrium face the same decision problem as the firms in the stringent equilibrium. The same is not true of the loose equilibrium, so that the fish-and-pond equilibrium can exist absent the loose equilibrium.

Existence of the stringent equilibrium, however, does not imply the existence of the fish-and-ponds equilibrium. The reason is that additional conditions are needed to ensure that workers self-select into ponds. These conditions require that λ not be too high. For workers who receive an unfavorable ability signal, the benefit from selecting a small pond is that every worker gets promoted, so that workers’ possibly low ability is not revealed to the market. If λ approaches 1, however, this benefit disappears, because workers would then essentially reveal their low ability by selecting the small pond. In this case, workers receiving a negative signal about their ability would always deviate from the proposed equilibrium by selecting a big pond.

The preceding discussion implies that multiple equilibria are possible for a given set of parameter values. An equilibrium refinement is applied to resolve multiple equilibria for the regions of the parameter space in which they occur. Specifically, efficiency is used as an equilibrium selection criterion. The idea is that if a more rather than a less efficient equilibrium is played, then additional surplus is created, which could be allocated among the players so as to make everyone better off. Therefore, using efficiency as a selection criterion is closely related to the well-known concept of payoff dominance (Harsanyi and Selten 1988).

Of the equilibria described in the preceding three propositions, the loose equilibrium is the most efficient, the stringent equilibrium is the least efficient, and the fish-and-ponds equilibrium lies in between. The reason follows from the condition c2+d2aL≥c1+d1aL⁠, which ensures that a worker should always be promoted on efficiency grounds, regardless of ability. Using efficiency as an equilibrium selection criterion, the loose equilibrium is played whenever it exists, the fish-and-ponds equilibrium is played whenever it exists alongside the stringent equilibrium but without the loose equilibrium, and the stringent equilibrium is played whenever it is unique. The result that workers are always promoted in the loose equilibrium derives from the simplifying assumption of binary ability. When that assumption is relaxed, as discussed at the start of Section 4, non-promoted workers can exist in this equilibrium as well as in the stringent and fish-and-ponds equilibria.

Two standard and popular equilibrium refinements might be considered as alternatives to the preceding efficiency refinement, though neither are helpful in this model. The first is the intuitive criterion, proposed by Cho and Kreps (1987).12 The second is coalition proofness (Bernheim et al. 1987). A formal analysis of this refinement is not pursued because it would be prohibitively complex, given that a large number of potential coalitions is possible. Nonetheless, the fish-and-ponds equilibrium appears not to be coalition proof and neither is the stringent equilibrium that (by the preceding corollary) always appears alongside it.13 Therefore, coalition proofness cannot be used to rank these two equilibria.

The fact that the fish-and-ponds equilibrium is never unique (because it always exists alongside the stringent equilibrium) raises the question of why many real-world settings appear to exhibit the fish-and-ponds phenomenon. This can be answered in two ways. First, as noted, using efficiency as an equilibrium refinement implies that the fish-and-ponds equilibrium will be chosen over the stringent equilibrium. The refinement is most applicable in settings in which the players can communicate and use that communication to coordinate on the efficient equilibrium. Although direct communication will not always be possible in every setting, tacit communication should often be possible in the Internet age in which there is voluminous publicly available information posted to and by employers and workers. Second, although the model assumes that firms are ex ante identical, in reality there could be firm heterogeneity for pre-determined reasons. If in the high-level job there is production function heterogeneity in the sensitivity of workers’ outputs to their abilities, then the fish-and-ponds equilibrium can be unique. Footnote 11 elaborates.

3.4 Analysis of Equilibrium Existence Conditions

Many parameters affect the existence and coexistence of the three equilibria and it is not possible to unambiguously determine which equilibria coexist when a given parameter is continuously varied while the others remain fixed. Nonetheless, some progress is possible. The loose equilibrium exists and is unique when the parameter configurations are such that workers are much more productive in job 2 than in job 1, so that firms greatly benefit from promoting workers. In contrast, the stringent equilibrium exists and is unique for parameter configurations such that the productivity gain from promotion is relatively low. Finally, when the productivity gain from promotion is intermediate, other possibilities arise, but the fish-and-ponds equilibrium can never exist alone, nor can it coexist with the loose equilibrium but absent the stringent equilibrium. Moreover, all three equilibria can simultaneously coexist. It is also possible that the two symmetric equilibria exist in the absence of the fish-and-ponds equilibrium. Recall, however, that a unique equilibrium results when efficiency is applied as a refinement.

Graphical representations of how existence changes across different regions of the parameter space are enlightening. For example, Figure 2 varies S and λ simultaneously, holding all others fixed at particular values.

Open in new tabDownload slide

When S is sufficiently high, the loose equilibrium exists and is unique, and when S is sufficiently low, the stringent equilibrium exists and is unique. Existence of these two equilibria does not depend on λ. While this observation is generally true for the stringent equilibrium, for the loose equilibrium it is driven by the choice of pL = 0.5, for the following reason: Since firms promote all of their workers in the loose equilibrium, the external firms do not learn anything new about the promoted workers’ abilities, meaning that their period-2 wage offer to these workers depends on the unconditional expectation of ability, which can be written as λλλλE[aj]=pL(λaL+(1−λ)aH)+(1−pL)((1−λ)aL+λaH)⁠. The higher this expectation, the higher the external firms’ period-2 wage offers and the lower the incumbent firm’s payoff from promoting a low-ability worker, making the loose equilibrium less likely to exist. For pL = 0.5, the expectation becomes E[aj]=0.5(aL+aH)⁠, which is independent of λ, as previously indicated. In contrast, for pL > 0.5, it would be decreasing in λ, with the result that the loose equilibrium would be more likely to exist if λ is high, while the opposite would be true for pL < 0.5.

The fish-and-ponds equilibrium exists only if both S and λ are neither too small nor too large. If S is large, then the gain from promoting a worker is so high that the big-pond firms wish to deviate by promoting all of their workers. Similarly, if S is low, the small-pond firms have an incentive to deviate by reassigning their low-ability workers to job 1 rather than promoting these workers. If λ is relatively high, then the big-pond firms are relatively confident of hiring high-ability workers and, thus, offer high wages to their workers. Here, the workers receiving the unfavorable ability signal wish to deviate by joining a big-pond firm instead of a small-pond firm. If λ is very low, big-pond firms are not very confident of hiring high-ability workers, so that the corresponding wages are low. Now the workers observing a favorable ability signal find it beneficial to deviate by joining a small-pond firm.

Most of the results depicted in Figure 2 hold in general and are not specific to the parameter values selected. In particular, when S is sufficiently high, the loose equilibrium exists and is unique. When S drops below a threshold, other possibilities arise, but the fish-and-ponds equilibrium can never exist alone, nor can it coexist with the loose equilibrium but absent the stringent equilibrium. Although Figure 2 suggests that a sufficiently low S is both a necessary and sufficient condition for the stringent and fish-and-ponds equilibria, in general it is only a necessary condition. For example, and in contrast to the fixed parameter values in Figure 2, suppose that the model’s parameters are such that a low-ability worker is far more productive in job 2 than in job 1. Then employers might wish to promote that worker even if S = 0. Therefore, if S becomes sufficiently low, then, depending on the other parameter values, it might happen that all three equilibria simultaneously coexist, but it could also be that only the symmetric equilibria exist or that only the loose equilibrium exists.

The conditions necessary for the fish-and-ponds equilibrium to exist are considerably more expansive when the baseline model is extended to incorporate workers’ overconfidence about their abilities, as shown in the next section.

4. Extensions

Two extensions of the baseline model are presented formally, in Sections 4.1 and 4.2. Three others are briefly and informally summarized beforehand, with elaboration and formal analyses available upon request. First, the simplifying assumption of binary ability from the baseline model implies, unrealistically, that all workers in small ponds get promoted in equilibrium. If a third “very low” ability level is introduced, along with three possible values for the ability signal that workers receive, then for some parameter configurations a fish-and-ponds equilibrium exists with similar properties to those of the baseline model, but in which the lowest-ability workers are not promoted, even in small ponds. Then the fact that non-promoted workers exist in both types of ponds means that period-2 wages can be compared in both job levels and are always higher in big than in small ponds.

Second, after period-1 wage offers are made and workers join firms, the workers can make costly investments in their general human capital. A worker whose initial ability is low could still achieve high ability due to the investment and this happens with some constant probability. The investment is undertaken during period 1 and, thus, affects only period-2 output. Apart from this difference in the timing of when these human capital investments yield productivity returns, they can be thought of as effort choices. As in the baseline model’s equilibrium, workers who receive the low ability signal choose a small pond, whereas those receiving the high ability signal choose a big pond. Workers who join a small pond never make human capital investments, whereas those who join a big pond invest when the cost of doing so is sufficiently low. Those investments increase the likelihood of a promotion and the accompanying wage increase.

Third, workers’ preferences for promotion are incorporated into the model to reflect the fact that workers’ desire to get promoted sometimes extends beyond the wage increases that are expected to accompany promotion. This extension creates the possibility that a worker who has sufficiently strong preferences for getting promoted might choose the small pond even when receiving a high ability signal. Although symmetric equilibria also exist, all of the extensions exhibit an asymmetric equilibrium in which big and small ponds coexist and the different types of firms target different types of workers.

4.1 A Constraint on the Number of Managers

In the present extension, the modeling assumptions are the same as in the main model except when otherwise noted. The goal is to show that big-pond firms can be bigger in size than small-pond firms. The starting point is the observation that, in some real-world settings, firms must fill a certain number of managerial positions to operate efficiently. The following additional constraint ensures that firms promote a certain number of workers with sufficiently high probability when they execute their promotion policy:
δP(npi≥n^)≥δ,
where npi is the number of workers that firm i promotes when executing its promotion policy, and n^∈N and δδ∈(0,1) are given. There are nL workers who observe the low-ability signal, σL, and nH workers who observe the high-ability signal, σH. Define λλδn^H:=min{n∈N:∑k=n^n(nk)λk(1−λ)n−k≥δ} and assume that nLn^≥2 and nHn^H≥2⁠. Notice that n^H≥n^ and that the inequality is strict for sufficiently large δ. For expositional convenience, it is assumed that both nLn^ and nHn^H are integers and that nLn^+nHn^H=N⁠. These assumptions imply that, in the equilibrium presented below, all firms actively employ workers, all small-pond firms are of the same size, and all big-pond firms are of the same size.14

The following proposition characterizes a fish-and-ponds equilibrium akin to the one from Proposition 3. The important observation is that the big-pond firms are bigger in size than the small-pond firms (⁠n^H relative to n^⁠). The reason is that they promote fewer of their workers, meaning that they need to hire more workers upfront to ensure that the managerial positions are staffed.

 
Proposition 4

There is a nonempty set of parameters under which there exists an asymmetric separating equilibrium (i.e., a “fish-and-ponds equilibrium”) with the following properties:

(a) In period 1, small-pond firms i∈{1,…,nLn^} all offer each worker a wage of w1SP⁠, whereas big-pond firms i∈{nLn^+1,…,N} all offer a wage of w1BP⁠.

(b) Each worker j observing σσσj=σL accepts the offer of one of the small-pond firms, such that each of these firms hires n^ workers.

Each worker j observing σσσj=σH accepts the offer of one of the big-pond firms, such that each of these firms hires n^H workers.

(c) (i) When worker j is hired by some small-pond firm i∈{1,…,nLn^}⁠, this firm always promotes the worker at the end of period 1.

(ii) All firms offer the worker a period-2 wage of w2SP⁠.

(iii) When worker j is hired by some big-pond firm i∈{nLn^+1,…,N}⁠, this firm promotes the worker at the end of period 1 if and only if aj = aH.

(iv) If the worker is promoted, all firms offer the worker a period-2 wage of w22BP(>w2SP)⁠. If the worker is not promoted, all firms offer a wage of w21BP(<w22BP)⁠.

(d) With probability γ1−γ⁠, the worker accepts their period-1 employer’s offer. With probability γ, the worker randomly accepts an external firm’s offer.

Point (b) says that, in equilibrium, the number of workers in big-pond firms is (weakly) larger than the number of workers in small-pond firms, and for sufficiently large δ the “weakly” can be dropped. In equilibrium, the fraction of small ponds is nLn^N and the fraction of big ponds is 1−nLn^N⁠. Thus, the fraction of small ponds is increasing in the number of workers who observe the low-ability signal.

The constraint δP(npi≥n^)≥δ ensures that firms promote a certain number of workers with sufficiently high probability. In practice, however, a constraint could also come from limited managerial positions. In this case, the constraint would be of the form δP(npi≤n^)≥δ⁠. The implications of the alternative constraint for firm size are the same as those just discussed. Again, big-pond firms are bigger in size than small-pond firms. The reason is that small-pond firms promote all of their workers, whereas big-pond firms promote only those who have high ability. Accordingly, big-pond firms can hire more workers relative to small-pond firms before the constraint binds.

4.2 Worker Overconfidence and Underconfidence

Choosing a big pond is inherently risky from the standpoint of promotion probability and a worker’s degree of confidence in their ability can be expected to influence their willingness to assume that risk. Even if attention is restricted to the set of workers who have received positive information about their abilities, those who lack confidence might choose the small pond to minimize the risk of not getting promoted. This is a particularly interesting dimension of worker heterogeneity to examine, both because overconfidence is a realistic consideration for the study of selection into big ponds and because it considerably expands the set of parameter configurations for which the fish-and-ponds equilibrium exists.

To incorporate these ideas into the baseline model, denote the probabilities σσλP(aH|σH)=P(aL|σL)=λ and σσλP(aH|σL)=P(aL|σH)=1−λ as the objective, that is, true, probabilities that workers have a specific ability level given their observed signal. Firms know these probabilities, but they do not know which signal a worker observed. Suppose that workers differ in how they interpret their ability signals. “Optimistic” (or overconfident) workers overestimate the probability that they have high ability; for these workers, σλλPopt(aH|σH)=λHO≥λ and σλλλPopt(aH|σL)=λLO∈[1−λ,λHO)⁠. “Pessimistic” (or underconfident) workers underestimate the probability that they have high ability; for these workers σλλλPpes(aH|σH)=λHP∈(λLP,λ] and σλλPpes(aH|σL)=λLP≤1−λ⁠. The baseline model emerges as a special case if λλλλHO=λHP=λ and λλλλLO=λLP=1−λ⁠.

An alternative modeling approach would introduce worker heterogeneity in the degree of risk aversion concerning income. Such an approach is not pursued here but could be expected to yield similar results. Workers who are extremely risk averse would always opt for the small pond where there is no income risk. Thus, a fish-and-ponds equilibrium could exist in which only workers who receive favorable ability signals and who are not very risk averse self-select into big ponds, whereas other workers choose small ponds.

Let qj∈{O,P} denote a variable indicating whether worker j is optimistic (⁠qj=O⁠) or pessimistic (⁠qj=P⁠) about their ability. Furthermore, let pHO denote the probability that a worker j observes the signal σH and that they are optimistic about their ability, and define pLO analogously. Likewise, denote by pHP the probability that a worker j observes the signal σH and is pessimistic about their ability, and define pLP analogously, where pHO+pLO+pHP+pLP=1⁠.

For brevity, only the asymmetric equilibrium is presented. As the following proposition shows, an equilibrium can exist in which big ponds target optimistic workers who observe a favorable ability signal, whereas small ponds target all other worker types. 

Proposition 5

There is a nonempty set of parameters under which there exists an asymmetric separating equilibrium (i.e., a “fish-and-ponds equilibrium”) with the following properties:

(a) In period 1, small-pond firms i∈{1,…,ı^} (with ı^∈{2,…,N−2}⁠) all offer each worker a wage of w1SPoc⁠, whereas big-pond firms i∈{ı^+1,…,N} all offer a wage equal to w1BPoc⁠.

(b) (i) If σσσσ(σj,qj)∈{(σL,O),(σL,P),(σH,P)}⁠, worker j accepts each offer of small-pond firms i∈{1,...,ı^} with the same probability 1ı^⁠.

(ii) If σσ(σj,qj)=(σH,O)⁠, worker j accepts each offer of big-pond firms i∈{ı^+1,…,N} with the same probability 1N−ı^⁠.

(c) (i) When worker j is hired by some small-pond firm i∈{1,...,ı^}⁠, this firm always promotes the worker at the end of period 1.

(ii) All firms offer the worker a period-2 wage of w2SPoc⁠.

(iii) When worker j is hired by big-pond firm i∈{ı^+1,…,N}⁠, this firm promotes the worker at the end of period 1 if and only if aj = aH.

(iv) If the worker is promoted, all firms offer the worker a period-2 wage of w22BPoc(>w2SPoc)⁠. If the worker is not promoted, all firms offer a wage of w21BPoc(<w22BPoc)⁠.

(d) With probability γ1−γ⁠, the worker accepts their period-1 employer’s offer. With probability γ, the worker randomly accepts an external firm’s offer.

Again, workers self-select into firms, choosing a small pond either if they receive an unfavorable signal or if they receive a favorable signal but are pessimistic and, thus, underestimate their probability of having high ability. In both cases, they believe that they are unlikely to succeed in a big pond and, thus, prefer to work in a small pond. Existence of the equilibrium requires that λHO and λHP be sufficiently different, since otherwise the worker types σ(σH,O) and σ(σH,P) cannot be separated.

Figure 3 graphs the region of the (S,λ) parameter space for which the fish-and-ponds equilibrium exists. Compared with Figure 2, the existence region is considerably expanded.

Open in new tabDownload slide

Asymmetric equilibria other than the one described in Proposition 5 may also exist. In particular, an equilibrium may exist in which underconfident workers who observe the low-ability signal choose the small pond, and all other workers choose the big pond. 

Proposition 5 has several interesting implications. Some talented workers—the σ(σH,O) types—choose big ponds, while others—the σ(σH,P) types—choose small ponds. Workers who choose small ponds are not necessarily less talented than those who choose big ponds, but they are less confident in their abilities, which makes them doubt that they can prevail in big ponds. Since choosing the big pond lets workers signal their favorable ability assessment, big ponds again pay higher period-2 wages than small ponds (in job 2).

The period-1 wages in Proposition 5 cannot be ranked, because the same two competing effects are present that were discussed in the context of the baseline model. The period-1 wage is expected to be higher in the big pond than in the small one if low-ability workers are only slightly more productive in job 2 than in job 1. The advantage of the small pond is efficient assignment of workers to jobs, meaning that even low-ability workers get promoted. If that advantage is sufficiently small, then the period-1 wage should be relatively higher in the big pond. That argument, however, assumes that the equilibrium always exists. If workers’ productivities are changed, then it is conceivable that at some point the equilibrium fails to exist.

5. Empirical Implications and Evidence

Most of what is believed concerning the fish-and-ponds phenomenon is not based on systematic empirical evidence but rather on anecdotes and widely accepted conventional wisdom gleaned from casual observation. For that reason, theoretical work on the fish-and-ponds problem has tended to evaluate model predictions against such conventional wisdom rather than against systematic empirical evidence. Morgan et al. (2018), for example, appeal entirely to “common intuition” when evaluating the predictions of their theoretical model. In addition to appealing to common intuition, we connect our theoretical predictions to evidence by identifying specific examples that match our theoretical predictions and by evaluating the model’s predictions against systematic empirical evidence using a proxy for pond size.

5.1 Firm Size as a Proxy for Pond Size

Linking the model’s predictions to systematic empirical evidence is facilitated by drawing on firm size as a proxy for pond size, a relationship which itself is an empirical prediction implied in Section 4.1. The proxy broadens the set of empirical facts that can be compared with the model’s predictions, given that the empirical literature on promotions and pay contains a lot of evidence concerning firm size, whereas the concept of pond size has not been operationalized empirically. Firm size is a natural proxy for pond size because big ponds (in the sense of prestige and competitiveness) tend to also be big in the literal sense of size. For example, the Big Four accounting firms (Deloitte, EY, PWC, and KPMG) are universally recognized as big ponds within the industry in the sense of prestige and they are also the four biggest firms in the industry in terms of size. Proposition 4 formalizes this connection between pond size and firm size. The theoretical result there is that in equilibrium, in the presence of a constraint on the number of managerial jobs, big ponds are larger in size than small ponds.

Firm size offers two further advantages as a proxy for pond size. First, it is an objective measure, whereas prestige is inherently subjective. Second, it is not binary and is treated as a continuous variable in empirical models. The problem with a binary labeling of some firms as big ponds and others as small ones is that these concepts are relative. Consider the following example from Morgan et al. (2018: 1634): “A freshly minted law graduate may have a choice between a ‘white shoe’ law firm in New York or a slightly less competitive and less lucrative firm in Philadelphia.” Readers can easily discern from this example that the New York firm is the big pond and the Philadelphia one the small. But relative to a small law firm in Tuscaloosa, the Philadelphia firm would be a big pond and the most elite law firm in the world might make even the New York firm look like a small pond.

The preceding discussion notwithstanding, firm size is not a perfect proxy for pond size. There are examples of elite, competitive organizations that have high standards but that are not large in size. There also exist institutional factors that, while independent of promotion policies, relate to firm size and can influence workers’ choice of firms. An example is employer-provided training, which may be more valuable for high-ability workers and which large firms can provide more efficiently than small firms. A further issue is that large firms’ potentially better connections to colleges and universities facilitate access to talent pools that smaller firms lack. This would allow large firms (even if they are not large ponds that apply stringent promotion standards) to attract a higher-ability workforce. Despite these limitations, our view is that firm size and pond size are likely to have a strong enough positive correlation to render the proxy informative.

5.2 Evidence of the Fish-and-Ponds Phenomenon

The fish-and-ponds equilibrium has four empirical implications that are consistent with observation. First, big and small ponds can coexist in equilibrium. Second, workers who receive favorable ability signals choose big ponds, whereas workers who receive unfavorable ability signals choose small ponds. Third, both high- and low-ability workers (in the sense of realized ability) can be found in both types of ponds. Fourth, managerial wage levels are higher in big than in small ponds, which follows from part (c) of Proposition 3, specifically a comparison of points (ii) and (iv).

As discussed in Section 1, all four predictions hold in the accounting industry. A second specific example concerns the labor market for corporate executives. Using firm size as a proxy for pond size, it is clear that large and small firms co-exist and compete in the same labor market for executive talent. Moreover, the most talented executives tend to become CEOs at large firms, though some small firms have great CEOs.15 In the empirical literature on executive compensation, it is well documented that CEO pay is increasing in firm size. Murphy (1999: 2493) refers to this phenomenon as “the best documented stylized fact regarding CEO pay: CEO pay is higher in larger firms.”

There is also empirical evidence that small firms (ponds) are more likely to use seniority-based promotion systems, which offer one interpretation for the promotion rules that are used by small-pond firms in the theoretical model. Mills (1985) analyzes data from an employer survey of 337 companies in which respondents were asked about how their last few promotion decisions were made. The dependent variable is a direct measure of seniority-based promotions, that is, whether the promoted worker had been the contender who had the longest service at the firm. One of the important predictors of that variable is the size of the production unit. Specifically, and consistent with the theoretical model, those that employed fewer than 1000 employees were 14% more likely to have promoted the most senior internal applicant.

In settings in which firm-specific human capital is important, it will more frequently happen that the most senior internal applicant (who has been around the longest and who, therefore, has likely accumulated the most firm-specific human capital) will also be the best candidate on grounds of merit. This, however, is not always so. In the aforementioned survey, in the 46 cases in which managers reported feeling required to select the most senior internal applicant, 41% reported that they passed over a higher-performing candidate based on current performance, and a third reported that they passed over a candidate with greater potential.

If the theoretical model were extended to an overlapping generations setting, a further prediction would emerge concerning an organization’s span of control. Specifically, the ratio of promoted workers to all workers is smaller in big ponds than in small ones. If one assumes that a new cohort of workers is hired into job 1 in each period, this implication is equivalent to the result that the span of control is larger in big than in small ponds. Empirical evidence that span of control is positively correlated with firm size dates back roughly half a century (e.g., Rushing 1966; Blau and Schoenherr 1971; Kasarda 1974), with more recent evidence provided in DeVaro and Morita (2013).

6. Conclusion

Common intuition holds that talented workers who are confident in their abilities tend to embrace the challenge of joining highly competitive organizations where the promotion prospects are uncertain but the potential rewards are great. Sometimes, however, such workers prefer to be big fish in small ponds. The fish-and-ponds metaphor is universally known in the context of informal discussions of careers, yet it has not been incorporated into the theoretical literature on promotion and wage dynamics. The present analysis shows that enrichments of the standard theoretical frameworks in that literature—that are natural and appealing from the standpoint of realism—give rise to equilibrium behaviors that are consistent with the fish-and-ponds phenomenon. Predictions of the fish-and-ponds framework can also explain a range of empirical phenomena.

3

Prior usage of the fish-and-ponds terminology differs somewhat from its usage in the model. In other contexts, it may refer to the relative rankings of individuals within organizations, with big fish defined as workers who are more talented or more productive than co-workers, or with a relatively higher standing in the organization’s hierarchy. For example, Elsner and Isphording (2017) find that students with a higher ordinal class rank are significantly more likely to complete high school and attend college. The authors argue that these higher-ranked students have higher expectations about their future careers, as well as higher perceived intelligence, which propels them to higher levels of human capital investment.

4

Representative theoretical contributions following the original study by Waldman (1984) include Ricart i Costa (1988), MacLeod and Malcomson (1988), Waldman (1990), Bernhardt (1995), Zábojník and Bernhardt (2001), Owan (2004), Ghosh and Waldman (2010), DeVaro and Waldman (2012), Gürtler and Gürtler (2019), and Waldman and Zax (2020).

5

Ekinci et al. (2019) analyze an alternative setup that incorporates worker effort choices and that models promotion-based and bonus-based incentives simultaneously, where the bonus is based on the amount by which the worker’s per-period output (which itself is linear in the worker’s effort and innate ability) exceeds a minimum output target set by the employer.

6

If (employer) learning after period 1 is imperfect (e.g., if the employer receives a noisy signal about ability rather than observing it exactly), this would complicate the analysis but should not qualitatively change the main results. Such an extension could also incorporate worker effort choices. Specifically, workers might exert effort to manipulate the information that their own employers receive about their abilities. Such an extension would be similar to the one concerning workers’ human capital investments (informally discussed in Section 4). Workers would not exert any effort in small ponds, but they might exert effort in big ponds to pretend that they have high ability and to increase their promotion chances.

7

If the assumption were dropped, the same equilibrium would exist, where the highest equilibrium offer by an external firm equals the worker’s expected productivity. However, the equilibrium would not be unique and other outcomes of the period-2 bargaining would be possible as well. Furthermore, the assumption that γ is independent of worker ability eliminates the strong winner’s curse result that evokes Milgrom and Oster (1987) and that occurs in other asymmetric learning models with firm-specific human capital and counteroffers (e.g., Ghosh and Waldman 2010; DeVaro and Waldman 2012; Cassidy et al. 2016; Waldman and Zax 2016). Finally, although the literature typically assumes that parameters like γ are small, this is not crucial for our results, as is clear from the proof of Proposition 3.

8

Notice that the wage in the low-level job may not be pinned down by equilibrium forces when the external firms expect the incumbent to always promote the worker. When studying such an equilibrium in Proposition 1, we show that the incumbent wishes to promote the worker even if external firms believe that a non-promoted worker has low ability for sure.

9

This assumption is implicit in the model, which focuses on a representative worker. It is also consistent with anti-discrimination laws that exist in many countries and that prohibit treating workers differently based on personal characteristics other than job performance. In the absence of this assumption, there could be an equilibrium in which a firm applies the loose promotion rule to some workers and the stringent one to others. Although career heterogeneity in the present model’s equilibria exists across firms rather than within them, in the real world career heterogeneity can arise because different promotion tracks exist within the same firm (e.g., a fast track and a regular track).

10

The same would be true if firms were allowed to mix between different wage offers. In period 2, the incumbent firm always matches the highest wage offer by the external firms. Therefore, the external firms compete in Bertrand fashion in that period, where their profits from hiring a worker are multiplied by γ. In period 1, all firms compete in Bertrand fashion as well. In analogy to Kaplan and Wettstein (2000), one can show that, since workers’ output is finite, a mixed-strategy equilibrium leading to a different outcome than the pure-strategy equilibrium does not exist. A proof is available from the authors upon request.

11

If firms are heterogeneous in their production technologies, it is conceivable that the fish-and-ponds equilibrium is unique for some parameter configurations. To see this, suppose that there are two types of firm with different production technologies in the high-level job. Moreover, let one type of firm have a large incentive to promote all workers regardless of their ability (e.g., due to a relatively large c2 and a relatively small d2⁠), whereas the other type promotes only workers who have high ability (e.g., due to a relatively small c2 and a large d2⁠). In this case, a fish-and-ponds equilibrium possibly exists, with workers who observe a negative ability signal selecting the first type of firm and the other workers selecting the second type. The stringent equilibrium, however, may not exist because of the first type’s incentive to promote all workers.

12

The intuitive criterion is unhelpful in the present context for the following reason. The fish-and-ponds equilibrium, for example, assumes that some firms offer w1SP in period 1 and others offer w1BP⁠, and all parties conclude that the former type of firm uses a loose and the latter a stringent promotion rule. Showing that no firm wishes to deviate from the equilibrium requires specifying what happens if a firm chooses a period-1 wage different from both w1SP and w1BP⁠. As an off-equilibrium belief, assume that all parties believe that the deviating firm would also use the stringent promotion rule. The intuitive criterion would now restrict the set of off-equilibrium beliefs, with the possible consequence that some equilibria no longer exist since they are supported by unreasonable beliefs. The intuitive criterion puts zero probability on those “types” whose equilibrium payoff is higher than the payoff they could achieve by the deviation for any off-equilibrium belief. The fact that all firms are ex ante identical and have the same equilibrium payoff of zero means that if any one of those firms were excluded by the intuitive criterion (or the corresponding promotion rule), all other firms would also need to be excluded. This is clearly not possible and eliminates the intuitive criterion as a candidate equilibrium refinement.

13

Consider, for example, the fish-and-ponds equilibrium and a coalition between a worker and a big-pond firm. Suppose that the worker, before learning their type, makes the following offer to the firm. The worker would join the firm upon receiving a high ability signal and would subsequently get promoted regardless of their ability realization; however, in the event of a low-ability realization, the worker would compensate the firm for that promotion. Given that promoting all workers is efficient, the payment could be chosen to make both parties better off, while all other players remain unaware of the coalition. Neither party to the coalition would have an incentive to deviate from this arrangement. Therefore, the equilibrium is not coalition proof.

14

If nLn^+nHn^H>N⁠, the number of firms would be small relative to the number of workers, with the consequence that the above constraint on the number of managers would be slack for some or all of the firms. Then the model would be very similar to the baseline model from Section 3, where big-ponds firms and small-pond firms cannot be ranked in terms of size. But whenever the constraint is binding for all of the active firms, such ranking is possible, and big-pond firms are indeed bigger in terms of size.

15

The number of CEOs who actually started working in the big-pond firm in which they ultimately became CEO speaks to how well the model describes CEO hiring. Given that the model features a 2-level job hierarchy, the relevant question is how often the CEOs of big-pond firms were promoted internally into that position as opposed to externally recruited into it. Consider the following 15 big-pond firms whose CEOs were among the most highly paid in 2018: GM, Ford, Oracle, Apple, McDonald’s, Lockheed Martin, Walmart, United Airlines, Microsoft, Lowe’s, AT&T, Kaiser Permanente, eBay, Target, and Uber. Thirteen of these 15 big-pond firms in 2018 had CEOs who were promoted from within. The only two that did not were Brian Cornell (CEO of Target) and Dara Khosrowshahi (CEO of Uber). For further information, see Sections 13.4 and 13.6 of DeVaro (2020).
