Appendix A

Proof of Proposition 1 Letting E[aj] denote workers’ expected ability, suppose that the model parameters satisfy the following two conditions:
(1+S)(c2+d2aL)≥c2+d2E[aj],
(A1)
(1+S)(c2−c1+(d2−d1)aL)≥d2(E[aj]−aL).
(A2)

The conditions are always jointly fulfilled for sufficiently high S. Wages are given by γγw1l=c1+(1−γ)Sc2+(d1+(1−γ)Sd2)E[aj] and w2l=c2+d2E[aj]⁠.

It must be shown that none of the parties wishes to deviate from the described behavior. First, consider the period-2 wage offers and workers’ acceptance decisions, assuming that the parties make the decisions described in parts (a) and (b) and that firms use the promotion rules described in part (c).

Since all wage offers are equally high, it immediately follows that workers stay with the incumbent firm with probability γ1−γ and switch to some other firm with probability γ. Recall that it is efficient to assign a worker to job 2 regardless of the worker’s ability. Hence, a firm that successfully poached a worker would always find it optimal to assign that worker to job 2. It is then straightforward to see that the external firms’ period-2 wage offers are always equal to the output that they could expect from a worker in job 2 if they could successfully poach that worker from the incumbent firm. Hence, the external firms’ expected period-2 profit is just zero. An external firm could not increase the profit by unilaterally deviating to a lower wage (since the firm would then never hire the worker) or a higher wage (since the firm would then offer a wage higher than the worker’s expected output). It follows that the external firms do not have an incentive to deviate from the specified period-2 wage offers.

Consider now firms’ wage offers to their own workers. Since firms always manage to retain their workers (unless they mistakenly fail to make a counteroffer), they do not have an incentive to offer anything higher. Condition (A1) implies that they make positive profit in period 2. Thus, they do not have an incentive to reduce the wage offer, because they would then definitely lose the workers.

The next step is to verify that firms do not wish to deviate from the promotion rules that are specified in the proposition’s part (c). If a firm were to hire a worker j with ability aL, the firm’s period-2 profit from promoting the worker would be
γ(1−γ)((1+S)(c2+d2aL)−w2l).
Likewise, the firm’s period-2 profit when reassigning the worker to job 1 would be
γmax{(1−γ)((1+S)(c1+d1aL)−w˜),0},
where w˜ is the wage that the firm would need to pay to retain worker j if it (unexpectedly) does not promote him or her. Since the external firms are willing to promote the worker even if they believe that the worker’s ability is aL, they offer a wage at least equal to c2+d2aL⁠. Thus, w˜≥c2+d2aL⁠.
If (1+S)(c1+d1aL)−(c2+d2aL)≤0⁠, the incumbent firm wishes to promote the worker for any w˜≥c2+d2aL⁠. Likewise, if (1+S)(c1+d1aL)−(c2+d2aL)>0 and
(1+S)(c2+d2aL)−w2l≥(1+S)(c1+d1aL)−c2−d2aL⇔(1+S)(c2−c1+(d2−d1)aL)≥d2(E[aj]−aL),
that is, if Condition (A2) holds, the firm again wishes to promote the worker for any w˜≥c2+d2aL⁠. Since the benefit from promoting a high-ability worker is higher than that from promoting a low-ability worker, the condition also ensures that the firm wishes to promote a high-ability worker.

Next, consider the workers’ acceptance decisions from the proposition’s part (b), assuming that firms made the period-1 wage offers specified in part (a). In equilibrium, workers correctly anticipate the firms’ decisions from part (c). Therefore, they anticipate that all firms adopt the same promotion rules. Given that all firms offer the same period-1 wage, workers are indifferent between all the firms’ offers, so that it is optimal for workers to accept each of the offers with the same probability.

Next, consider the firms’ wage offers from the proposition’s part (a). The wages are determined such that all firms receive zero expected profit, because a firm’s expected profit can be stated as
γγγγc1+d1E[aj]−w1l+(1−γ)((1+S)(c2+d2E[aj])−w2l)=c1+d1E[aj]−c1−(1−γ)Sc2−(d1+(1−γ)Sd2)E[aj]+(1−γ)((1+S)(c2+d2E[aj])−c2−d2E[aj])=0.

It must therefore be shown that firms cannot earn a strictly positive expected profit by deviating from the wage offer w1l⁠. To do so, the parties’ off-equilibrium beliefs must first be determined in case firms deviate from the period-1 wage offers stated in the proposition. In particular, one set of off-equilibrium beliefs must be determined that supports the equilibrium proposed in the proposition. In this context, it is assumed that if a firm deviates from the wage offer w1l⁠, all parties believe that the firm still promotes all workers regardless of their abilities. Note that here, and in the other propositions, the parties’ beliefs must be explicitly specified in the case of a deviation, since different promotion rules could possibly be sustained in equilibrium. Given that preceding assumption concerning beliefs, one can show that a unilateral deviation from the proposed equilibrium is not profitable. If a firm were to unilaterally deviate to some wage lower than w1l⁠, the firm would never successfully hire a worker. If a firm were to unilaterally deviate to some wage higher than w1l⁠, the firm would possibly hire a worker but would pay a total expected wage higher than the worker’s total expected output, thus making a loss. ■

Proof of Proposition 2 Suppose that the model parameters satisfy the following three conditions:
(1+S)(c1+d1aL)≥c2+d2aL,
(A3)
w22s−w21s≥(1+S)(c2−c1+(d2−d1)aL),
(A4)
w22s−w21s≤(1+S)(c2−c1+(d2−d1)aH).
(A5)

The wages are given by γλλw1s=c1+d1E[aj]+(1−γ)((pHλ+pL(1−λ))S(c2+d2aH))γλλ+(1−γ)((pH(1−λ)+pLλ)((1+S)(c1+d1aL)−c2−d2aL)), w22s=c2+d2aH⁠, and w21s=c2+d2aL.

The proof is analogous to that of Proposition 1. It can immediately be seen that workers always stay with their period-1 employer with probability γ1−γ and switch firms with probability γ.

External firms are able to infer workers’ abilities from the promotion decision and their period-2 wage offers are again equal to the output that they could expect from a worker in job 2 if they managed to poach the worker from the incumbent firm. As in the proof of Proposition 1, the external firms, thus, do not have an incentive to deviate from the specified period-2 wage offers.

Consider now firms’ wage offers to their own workers. Since firms always manage to retain their workers (unless they mistakenly fail to make a counteroffer), they do not have an incentive to offer a higher wage than that previously stated. Condition (A3) implies that they make positive profit in period 2 even if a worker is revealed to have low ability. Thus, they do not have an incentive to reduce the wage offer, because they would then definitely lose the worker.

The next step verifies that firms do not wish to deviate from the promotion rules that are specified in the proposition’s part (c). If a firm were to hire a (low-ability) worker j, the firm’s period-2 profit from reassigning the worker to job 1 would be
γ(1−γ)((1+S)(c1+d1aL)−w21s).
Likewise, the firm’s period-2 profit when promoting the worker to job 2 would be
γmax{(1−γ)((1+S)(c2+d2aL)−w22s),0}.

Condition (A4) ensures that the firm prefers to reassign the worker to job 1. Analogously, Condition (A5) ensures that, if the firm were to hire a worker j with ability aH, the firm would prefer to promote the worker to job 2.

Next, consider workers’ acceptance decisions from the proposition’s part (b), assuming that firms made the period-1 wage offers specified in part (a). In equilibrium, workers correctly anticipate the firms’ decisions from part (c). Therefore, they anticipate that all firms adopt the same promotion rules. Given that all firms offer the same period-1 wage, workers are indifferent among all the firms’ offers, so that it is optimal for workers to accept each of the offers with the same probability.

Next, consider the firms’ wage offers from the proposition’s part (a). Wages are determined such that all firms receive zero expected profit, because a firm’s expected profit can be stated as
γλλγλλγλλγλλγλλγλλc1+d1E[aj]−w1s+(1−γ)(pHλ+pL(1−λ))((1+S)(c2+d2aH)−w22s)+(1−γ)(pH(1−λ)+pLλ)((1+S)(c1+d1aL)−w21s)=c1+d1E[aj]−c1−d1E[aj]−(1−γ)(pHλ+pL(1−λ))S(c2+d2aH)−(1−γ)(pH(1−λ)+pLλ)((1+S)(c1+d1aL)−c2−d2aL)+(1−γ)(pHλ+pL(1−λ))((1+S)(c2+d2aH)−c2−d2aH)+(1−γ)(pH(1−λ)+pLλ)((1+S)(c1+d1aL)−c2−d2aL)=0.

It must, therefore, be shown that firms cannot earn a strictly positive expected profit from deviating to a different wage offer. To do so, the parties’ off-equilibrium beliefs must first be determined in case firms deviate from the period-1 wage offers stated in the proposition. In particular, one set of off-equilibrium beliefs must be determined that supports the equilibrium proposed in the proposition. In this context, it is assumed that, if a firm deviates from the wage offer w1s⁠, all parties believe that the corresponding firm still decides to promote a worker if and only if the worker has high ability. One can then show that a unilateral deviation from the proposed equilibrium is not profitable. When a firm unilaterally deviates to some wage lower than w1s⁠, the firm would never successfully hire a worker. When a firm unilaterally deviates to some wage higher than w1s⁠, the firm would possibly hire a worker but would pay a total expected wage higher than the worker’s total expected output, thus making a loss.

In the last step, it is shown that the stated Conditions(A3)–(A5) can be jointly satisfied. Suppose that
pL,pH>0,c1=8/3,c2=2,d1=1,d2=2,aL=2,aH=3, and S=0.5.
Inserting the wage formulas and the given parameter values into Conditions(A3)–(A5) yields
7≥6,2≥2,2≤7/2,
from which it is clear that all the conditions are met. ■
Proof of Proposition 3 Suppose that the model parameters satisfy Conditions (A3)–(A5) (with w21s and w22s replaced by w21BP and w22BP⁠) and the following three conditions:
(1+S)(c2+d2aL)−w2SP≥(1+S)(c1+d1aL)−c2−d2aL,
(A6)
λλw1SP+w2SP≥w1BP+(1−λ)w22BP+λw21BP,
(A7)
λλw1BP+λw22BP+(1−λ)w21BP≥w1SP+w2SP.
(A8)

The wages are given by γγλλγλλγλγλγw1SP=c1+(1−γ)Sc2+(d1+(1−γ)Sd2)(λaL+(1−λ)aH), w1BP=c1+(1−γ)(1+S)(λc2+(1−λ)c1)+(d1+(1−γ)Sd2)λaH+(d1+(1−γ)((1+S)d1−d2))(1−λ)aL−(1−γ)c2⁠, λλw2SP=c2+d2(λaL+(1−λ)aH), w22BP=c2+d2aH⁠, and w21BP=c2+d2aL⁠.

It must be shown that none of the parties wishes to deviate from the described behavior. The proof of part (d) is obvious. Furthermore, analogous to the argumentation in the proofs of the preceding propositions, none of the external firms has an incentive to deviate from the specified period-2 wage offers.

Consider now firms’ wage offers to their own workers. Since firms always manage to retain their workers (unless they mistakenly fail to make a counteroffer), they do not have an incentive to offer a higher wage. Notice that Conditions (A3) and (A6) together imply that (1+S)(c2+d2aL)≥w2SP⁠. Hence, for a small-pond firm i∈{1,…,ı^}⁠, the profit from retaining a worker in period 2 is always positive. This implies that the firm has no incentive to reduce the wage. Because of Condition (A3) the same is true for a big-pond firm i∈{ı^+1,…,N} and the proof is the same as the corresponding proof for Proposition 2.

The next step verifies that firms do not wish to deviate from the promotion rules that are specified in the proposition’s part (c). Condition (A6) ensures that each firm i∈{1,…,ı^} wishes to promote every worker regardless of ability, whereas Conditions (A4) and (A5) ensure that each firm i∈{ı^+1,…,N} wishes to promote a worker if and only if the worker has high ability. The corresponding proofs are analogous to those from the preceding propositions.

Turning next to the decisions from part (b), notice that firms, which are unable to observe the signals that workers receive, can never observe whether or not workers stuck to the decisions described in the proposition’s part (b). This means that, if a worker were to deviate from the acceptance decision, firms would be unaware of this deviation and would therefore not adapt their decisions from part (c). In equilibrium, workers correctly anticipate the firms’ decisions from part (c). If σσσj=σL⁠, it must be shown that worker j prefers to work for some firm i∈{1,…,ı^} rather than some firm i∈{ı^+1,…,N}⁠. So it must be shown that
λλw1SP+w2SP≥w1BP+(1−λ)w22BP+λw21BP,
which is implied by Condition (A7). If σσσj=σH⁠, it must be shown that worker j prefers to work for some firm i∈{ı^+1,…,N} rather than some firm i∈{1,…,ı^}⁠. Hence, it must be shown that
λλw1BP+λw22BP+(1−λ)w21BP≥w1SP+w2SP,
which is implied by Condition (A8).
Turning next to the firms’ wage offers from part (a) of the proposition, it is easy to see that the wages are determined such that all firms receive zero expected profit. To show this, consider first some firm i∈{1,…,ı^}⁠. The firm’s expected profit can be stated as
λλγλλλλγγλλγλλγλλc1+d1(λaL+(1−λ)aH)−w1SP+(1−γ)((1+S)(c2+d2(λaL+(1−λ)aH))−w2SP)=c1+d1(λaL+(1−λ)aH)−c1−(1−γ)Sc2−(d1+(1−γ)Sd2)(λaL+(1−λ)aH)+(1−γ)(1+S)(c2+d2(λaL+(1−λ)aH))−(1−γ)(c2+d2(λaL+(1−λ)aH))=0.
Similarly, for a firm i∈{ı^+1,…,N}⁠, the expected profit can be stated as
λλγλλλλγλλγλγλγγλγλc1+d1(λaH+(1−λ)aL)−w1BP+(1−γ)(λ((1+S)(c2+d2aH)−w22BP)+(1−λ)((1+S)(c1+d1aL)−w21BP))=c1+d1(λaH+(1−λ)aL)−c1−(1−γ)(1+S)(λc2+(1−λ)c1)−(d1+(1−γ)Sd2)λaH−(d1+(1−γ)((1+S)d1−d2))(1−λ)aL+(1−γ)c2+(1−γ)λ((1+S)(c2+d2aH)−c2−d2aH)+(1−γ)(1−λ)((1+S)(c1+d1aL)−c2−d2aL)=0.

It must therefore be shown that firms cannot earn a strictly positive expected profit from deviating to a different wage offer. To do so, it is necessary to first determine the parties’ off-equilibrium beliefs in case firms deviate from the period-1 wage offers stated in the proposition. In particular, one set of off-equilibrium beliefs must be determined that supports the equilibrium proposed in the proposition. Two different types of deviations from the period-1 offers are possible. First, it is possible that all firms either offer the wage w1SP or w1BP but that the number of firms offering w1SP (⁠w1BP⁠) differs from ı^ (⁠N−ı^⁠). In this case, it is assumed that all parties believe that a firm offering w1SP still decides to promote all workers at the end of period 1 regardless of their ability, whereas a firm offering w1BP only promotes those workers who are revealed to have high ability. It follows that a firm i∈{1,…,ı^} would never gain from deviating from the proposed equilibrium by offering the wage w1BP⁠. The reason is that, upon such a deviation, everyone would believe that the firm promotes only high-ability workers, implying that only workers with σσσj=σH would select this firm. In turn, the firm would find it optimal to promote only high-ability workers, leaving it still with zero expected profit. Analogously, none of the firms i∈{ı^+1,…,N} gains from unilaterally deviating from the proposed equilibrium by offering the wage w1SP⁠.

Second, it is possible that at least one firm deviates from the proposed equilibrium by offering some wage w1∈R\{w1SP,w1BP}⁠. In this case, it is assumed that all parties believe that the corresponding firm only promotes those workers who are revealed to have high ability. Hence, a worker thinking about selecting the firm would anticipate that their ability would be revealed to all parties after period 1 by the firm’s job assignment. Again, one can show that a unilateral deviation from the proposed equilibrium is not profitable. When a firm unilaterally deviates to some wage w1<w1BP (and w1≠w1SP⁠), the firm would never successfully hire a worker, because workers of types σL would prefer one of the firms offering w1SP and workers of type σH would prefer one of the firms offering w1BP⁠. When a firm unilaterally deviates to some wage w1>w1BP (and w1≠w1SP⁠), the firm would possibly hire a worker but would pay a total expected wage higher than the worker’s total expected output, thus making a loss.

In the last step, it is shown that the stated Conditions (A3)–(A8) can be jointly fulfilled. Suppose that
γλ0<γ≤23,λ=35,pL>0,pH>0,c1=83,c2=2,d1=1,d2=2,aL=2,aH=3, and S=0.5.
Inserting the above parameter values into the different wage formulas implies
γγλλγγγγγw1SP=c1+(1−γ)Sc2+(d1+(1−γ)Sd2)(λaL+(1−λ)aH)=83+(1−γ)·0.5·2+(1+(1−γ)·0.5·2)(35·2+25·3)=83+1−γ+(2−γ)·125=7615+(1−γ)·175
γλλγλγλγγγγγγγγγγλλw1BP=c1+(1−γ)(1+S)(λc2+(1−λ)c1)+(d1+(1−γ)Sd2)λaH+(d1+(1−γ)((1+S)d1−d2))(1−λ)aL−(1−γ)c2=83+(1−γ)·(1+0.5)·(35·2+25·83)+(1+(1−γ)·0.5·2)·35·3+(1+(1−γ)·((1+0.5)·1−2))·25·2−(1−γ)·2=83+(1−γ)·175+(2−γ)·95+45−25(1−γ)−(1−γ)·2=7915+(1−γ)·145w2SP=c2+d2(λaL+(1−λ)aH)=2+2(35·2+25·3)=345w22BP=c2+d2aH=2+2·3=8,w21BP=c2+d2aL=2+2·2=6.
From the proof of Proposition 2, we already know that Conditions (A3)–(A5) are satisfied with the above parameter values. Inserting the wage levels and the parameter values into Conditions (A6)–(A8) implies
λλγγγλλγγγ(1+S)(c2+d2aL)−w2SP≥(1+S)(c1+d1aL)−c2−d2aL⇔2.2=(1+0.5)(2+2·2)−345≥(1+0.5)(83+1·2)−2−2·2=1,w1SP+w2SP≥w1BP+(1−λ)w22BP+λw21BP ⇔7615+(1−γ)·175+345≥7915+(1−γ)·145+25·8+35·6⇔γ≤23, w1BP+λw22BP+(1−λ)w21BP≥w1SP+w2SP ⇔7915+(1−γ)·145+35·8+25·6≥7615+(1−γ)·175+345⇔γ≥0.

Consequently, all of Conditions (A3)–(A8) are satisfied. ■

Proof of Corollary 1 Assume that the fish-and-pond equilibrium exists. Condition (A3) is a necessary condition for this type of equilibrium to exist and is, therefore, fulfilled. Moreover, when the big-pond firms decide about the promotion decision, their decision problem is equivalent to firms’ corresponding decision problem in the stringent equilibrium from Proposition 2 (since the external firms’ wage offers are the same in the two types of equilibrium). Consequently, whenever the fish-and-ponds equilibrium exists, the big-pond firms do not wish to deviate from their promotion decisions, implying that the same is true for the firms in the stringent equilibrium, so that the latter type of equilibrium exists as well.

In Figure 2 in Section 3.4, we identify parameter constellations that lead to the existence of a fish-and-pond equilibrium, but for which no loose equilibrium exists, proving the second statement of the corollary. ■

Proof of Proposition 4 The constraint δP(npi≥n^)≥δ is met for either type of firm. Furthermore, the equilibrium behavior is almost identical to the one described in Proposition 3 (except that workers now select one of the firms with certainty in period 1 rather than selecting a firm randomly; as they are indifferent, however, this does not affect their incentive to deviate). The proof of the proposition is, therefore, analogous to the proof of Proposition 3. ■
